e.etymology: From the English word ocean, which goes back to Greek Okeanos, the great river thought to circle the world. Its use as a name follows the French girls' name Océane.
From an English surname for someone who lived near springs or wells, from Old English wella, 'spring'. Wells is also a cathedral city in Somerset.

assoc.t: first word of Wells Fargo, the bank

e.etymology: From an English and Scottish surname, a nickname for someone with red hair or a ruddy face, from Old English read, 'red'. It also matches the word for the tall marsh grass.
namesakes: Reed Richards (Mister Fantastic of the Fantastic Four)

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Cameron used mostly for girls. Cameron is the Scottish clan surname from Gaelic cam, 'crooked', and sròn, 'nose'.

e.meaning: poet or fawn (from an Irish surname)
e.etymology: From an Irish surname, anglicized from Ó Damháin or Ó Daimhín and linked to words for 'fawn' or 'poet'. It is also used as a variant of Devon, the English county.
namesakes: Devin Hester (NFL Hall of Fame return specialist)

e.etymology: From Arabic nasir, 'helper, one who gives victory', from the verb nasara, 'to help'.
A French short form of Nicolette, the feminine pet form of Nicolas, from Greek nike, 'victory', and laos, 'people'. Saint Colette of Corbie reformed the Poor Clares in the 15th century.
namesakes: Colette Tatou (the chef in Pixar's Ratatouille)

assoc.t: Colette, the French novelist who wrote Gigi

e.etymology: The French feminine form of Michel (Michael), from Hebrew Mikhael, 'who is like God?'. It was popular in the US from the 1960s to the 1990s, helped by the Beatles' song Michelle (1965).

assoc.t: Michelle, the 1965 Beatles ballad

e.meaning: varies by origin: a form of Cyrus, or Irish for dark-haired
e.etymology: A variant of Kyra or a borrowing of Russian Kira, both feminine forms of Cyrus, the Persian royal name. It is also used as a phonetic spelling of Irish Ciara, 'dark-haired'.

assoc.t: Kira, the killer's alias in the anime Death Note
Major Kira of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine

e.meaning: name of the Greek god of light, music and prophecy
e.etymology: From Greek Apollon, the god of light, music, healing and prophecy; the root of the name is unknown. NASA's Apollo program carried the name to the Moon.
namesakes: Apollo Creed (Rocky Balboa's rival and friend in the Rocky films)

assoc.t: Apollo program, NASA's Moon landing missions
Greek and Roman god of the sun, music and prophecy
Apollo Creed, the champion boxer in Rocky
Apollo Theater, the Harlem music hall

e.etymology: The Italian form of Alexandra, the feminine of Alexander, from Greek alexein, 'to defend', and aner, 'man'.
From the English word lyric, the words of a song or a short songlike poem, from Greek lyrikos, 'sung to the lyre'.
The Irish form of John, borrowed from Norman French Jehan and going back to Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
From an English surname with more than one source: a nickname from Old French tison, 'firebrand', for a hot-tempered person, or a variant of Dyson, 'son of Dennis'.

assoc.t: Mike Tyson, heavyweight boxing champion
Tyson Foods, the chicken and meat producer

e.etymology: Several names in one: a Slavic short form of names with mir, 'peace'; the name of the 16th-century Indian poet-saint Mirabai; and a short form of Miranda, from Latin mirus, 'wonderful'.

assoc.t: Mira, a red giant star in the constellation Cetus
Mira, a member of Huntr/x in KPop Demon Hunters

e.note: In Spanish, mira means 'look', so Spanish speakers hear the name as an everyday command.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Nechemyah, 'Yahweh comforts'. In the Bible Nehemiah is the governor who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
A 20th-century American coinage that joins Rae with the -lyn ending.
Taken from Kylo Ren, the villain of the Star Wars sequel films that began with The Force Awakens (2015). The name was invented for the character.

assoc.t: Kylo Ren, the villain of the Star Wars sequels

e.etymology: A Latin form of Greek Berenice, 'bringer of victory', reshaped by the church phrase vera icon, 'true image', tied to Saint Veronica, who wiped the face of Jesus on the road to Calvary.
namesakes: Veronica Lodge (heiress of Archie Comics and Riverdale)
Veronica Mars (teen detective of the TV series)

assoc.t: Veronica Lodge of Archie Comics and Riverdale
Veronica Mars, TV's teen private detective

e.etymology: From the Dakota word koda, 'friend', and also used as a short form of Dakota itself. Disney's Brother Bear (2003), with its bear cub Koda, brought it into use.

assoc.t: Koda, the bear cub in Disney's Brother Bear

e.etymology: A pet form of Frank and Francis for boys and of Frances and Francesca for girls, names that go back to Latin Franciscus, 'Frenchman'. It is now given as a full name, more often to girls.
namesakes: Frankie Valli (lead singer of the Four Seasons)
Frankie Muniz (star of Malcolm in the Middle)

e.etymology: A spelling of Mackenzie, the Scottish surname from Gaelic Mac Coinnich, 'son of Coinneach', a name meaning 'handsome' that is anglicized as Kenneth.
From a Norman surname, Old French bel ami, 'fair friend'. Its use as a first name grew after the character Bellamy Blake in the TV series The 100 (2014).
namesakes: Bellamy Blake (a lead character in The 100)

assoc.t: Bellamy Blake of the CW series The 100

e.meaning: sage: the herb, or a wise person
e.etymology: A spelling of Sage, the English word for both the fragrant herb, from Latin salvia, and a wise person, from Latin sapere, 'to be wise'.

assoc.t: Saige, American Girl's 2013 Girl of the Year doll

e.etymology: A spelling of Zane, a surname of uncertain origin that became a first name through Western novelist Zane Grey. Zane was his mother's maiden name; her family founded his hometown of Zanesville, Ohio.

assoc.t: sounds like Zayn, the former One Direction singer

e.etymology: An English spelling of Scandinavian Gunnar, from Old Norse gunnr, 'battle', and a second element meaning 'warrior'. The spelling matches the English word gunner, a soldier who mans a gun.
From Old High German Mahthilt, joining maht, 'might', and hild, 'battle'. The Normans brought it to England with William the Conqueror's queen, Matilda of Flanders.
namesakes: Matilda Wormwood (heroine of Roald Dahl's Matilda)
Empress Matilda (12th-century claimant to the English throne)

assoc.t: heroine of Roald Dahl's Matilda and its films
Waltzing Matilda, Australia's folk anthem
Matilda, the 2022 Harry Styles song

e.meaning: city of Alexander, defender of men
e.etymology: From the cities Alexander the Great founded and named for himself, above all Alexandria in Egypt. Alexander comes from Greek alexein, 'to defend', and aner, 'man'.
namesakes: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (US congresswoman from New York)

assoc.t: Egyptian port city founded by Alexander the Great
Alexandria, Virginia, just outside Washington, DC

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Callie, a pet form of names such as Caroline and Calista. It is also read as Cali, the nickname for California.

assoc.t: Cali, slang for California
Cali, a major city in Colombia

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Peter, from Greek petros, 'rock', the name Jesus gave the apostle Simon.
namesakes: Pedro Pascal (actor, The Mandalorian and The Last of Us)

assoc.t: Pedro of Napoleon Dynamite (Vote for Pedro)

e.meaning: combination of Anna, grace, and Lise, from Elizabeth
e.etymology: An English spelling of German Anneliese and Danish Anne-Lise, a compound of Anna, 'grace', and Liese or Lise, short forms of Elisabeth, 'God is my oath'.
namesakes: Annalise Keating (Viola Davis's lawyer in How to Get Away with Murder)

e.meaning: from Royse, a medieval form of Rose
e.etymology: From an English surname based on the medieval women's name Royse or Rose. The Rolls-Royce car gives it a ring of luxury.

assoc.t: second half of Rolls-Royce, the luxury car maker
